strengths: Novel demonstration of power law scaling for fMRI MAE models - first time exact power law observed in fMRI foundation models
Well-motivated intermediate data representation (flat maps) that elegantly balances information preservation with structural inductive bias
Rigorous experimental methodology with careful ablation studies on dataset size, model size, and temporal patch size; proper subject-based train/val/test splits
Strong performance on HCP state decoding (98.8%), substantially improving over prior work
Transparent reporting of limitations and work-in-progress status; honest discussion of OOD generalization weakness and data diversity issues
Comprehensive experimental protocol including in-distribution and out-of-distribution evaluation across three downstream tasks
Open science commitment with promised code and dataset release
Clear presentation with well-organized narrative and informative visualizations
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty - primarily applies existing spatiotemporal MAE techniques to new representation; minimal technical modifications required
Incomplete downstream evaluation acknowledged as 'preliminary' and 'signs of life' - UKBB sex classification actually underperforms prior work (84.6% vs Brain-JEPA's 88.6%)
Weak out-of-distribution generalization (Figure 3b) with performance saturation on NSD, suggesting scaling law does not generalize and raising fundamental questions about data diversity
No direct empirical comparison to alternative tokenization strategies (parcellation vs volumetric) despite this being central motivation
Difficult comparison to prior work due to different experimental protocols; patch embedding baseline achieves 94.1% on HCP, questioning whether improvements come from MAE pretraining
Unexplained empirical phenomena: small models (12.4M params) outperform large models (88.6M params and ViT-L), temporal patch size effects unexplained, computational implications ignored
Power law exponent extremely small (α=0.016) based on only 5 data points with questionable statistical reliability; confidence intervals missing
Limited representation quality analysis - no investigation of learned features, interpretability, or alignment with known brain networks
Missing direct comparisons to concurrent fMRI foundation models despite citing recent work; lacks analysis of why approach succeeds/fails relative to alternatives
Work-in-progress status with code unavailable; some implementation details unclear (e.g., CLIP benchmark construction relies on subjective UMAP inspection)

strengths: Thoughtful representation design: Flat maps provide an elegant middle ground between lossy parcellation and expensive 4D volumetric approaches, preserving full dimensionality while injecting cortical surface structure

Power law scaling observation: Demonstrates strict power law scaling of reconstruction loss with dataset size, supporting foundation model viability (though with significant caveats in out-of-distribution settings)
Multi-dataset evaluation framework: Uses HCP for pretraining and NSD/UKBB for generalization assessment, identifying meaningful distribution shift effects
Clear presentation: Well-written paper with informative visualizations of masked reconstructions and scaling behavior
Open science commitment: Promises code and data release supporting reproducibility and community contribution
weaknesses: CRITICAL: No direct comparison to alternative approaches—the paper explicitly positions flat maps against 4D volumetric (Kim et al. [16], Wang et al. [20]) and parcellation-based approaches but provides no empirical comparison. Authors acknowledge this gap as future work. Without comparisons, we cannot assess whether flat maps improve over alternatives or whether strong results are due to the representation specifically versus other factors like model scale.

Downstream results weaker than claimed: (1) HCP 98.8% vs patch embedding baseline 94.1% shows only 4.7% improvement from pretraining, with prior work ranging 93.4-94.8%; (2) UKBB 84.6% underperforms SOTA Brain-JEPA 88.6%; (3) NSD task uses arbitrary CLIP-assigned labels on acknowledged 'ambiguous, ill-posed' task. Claims of 'state of art performance attainable' are unsupported.

Scaling law concerns: (1) Exponent is very shallow (-0.016) compared to language models (-0.076 to -0.1), yielding minimal improvement per additional data; (2) fitted using only 5 data points; (3) out-of-distribution scaling shows clear saturation/deviation on NSD, with OOD power law fit using only first 3 points; (4) undermines foundation model narrative given acknowledged HCP diversity insufficiency.

Non-monotonic downstream generalization: Figure 4 (left) shows 3.2M frame model outperforming 7.4M on OOD benchmarks. This contradicts foundation model expectations and suggests the model learns HCP-specific patterns rather than generalizable representations, contradicting the paper's main narrative.

Limited methodological novelty: Uses standard ViT-MAE components (He et al. 2022) and spatiotemporal MAE (Wang et al. 2024). The only contribution is the flat map representation and excluding background patches—primarily an engineering contribution rather than methodological advance.

Suboptimal experimental design: Figure 4 (right) reveals smaller temporal patch sizes (pt=4,8) improve performance over default pt=16, suggesting results weren't fully optimized. Missing critical ablations on masking ratio, flat map resolution, global signal regression, and temporal resampling choices.

Incomplete evaluation: (1) Only 3 classification tasks with no clinical prediction validation despite clinical motivation; (2) Only frozen encoder evaluation via attentive probes; (3) No direct fine-tuning experiments; (4) No analysis of learned representations or failure cases.

Reproducibility gaps: Code/datasets promised with incomplete URL; custom NSD CLIP label assignment (41 categories) appears arbitrary and needs justification; many hyperparameter choices lack justification (clip length=16s, flat map resolution 224×560).

No statistical rigor: Missing confidence intervals, significance testing, or multiple testing correction. Error bars shown inconsistently in Figure 4. No investigation of whether performance differences are statistically meaningful.

Contradictory data diversity argument: Authors acknowledge 'HCP is insufficiently diverse to support learning truly generalizable representations' based on OOD saturation, yet continue to position this as viable foundation model work without addressing this fundamental limitation.

strengths: Clear problem motivation with well-reasoned intermediate representation (flat maps) between parcellation and 4D volume approaches
First empirical demonstration of power law scaling for fMRI foundation models, showing L ∝ N^(-0.016) on in-distribution HCP data
Rigorous experimental design with proper train/val/test splits, comprehensive ablations (dataset/model/temporal patch size), and in-distribution/out-of-distribution evaluation across three datasets
Honest and transparent limitations discussion acknowledging gaps in data diversity, scaling robustness, and missing comparisons to alternative approaches
Competitive downstream performance: 98.8% HCP cognitive state decoding, >8× chance on NSD CLIP classification, approaching prior art on UKBB sex classification
Strong reproducibility practices with detailed implementation appendix, promised code/data release, and clear preprocessing pipeline
Good open science practices and willingness to share code/datasets as ongoing project
weaknesses: No direct empirical comparisons to parcellation-based or 4D volumetric approaches despite positioning flat maps as an intermediate solution—this is the most significant gap, preventing validation of claimed advantages

Limited power law evidence: only 5 data points with very small exponent (0.016), and out-of-distribution scaling breaks down (Figure 3b), suggesting potential overfitting to HCP domain rather than genuine foundation model properties

Concerning generalization pattern: 3.2M-frame models match or exceed 7.4M performance on out-of-distribution tasks, contradicting scaling law claims and suggesting data diversity matters more than scale
Modest methodological novelty: primarily applies existing techniques (MAE, ViT, VideoMAE) to new representation with minimal technical adaptation (only excluding background pixels from loss)

Mixed downstream results undermine claims of superiority: UKBB sex classification (84.6%) lags Brain-JEPA (88.6%) and BrainLM (86.5%); HCP near-ceiling performance limits interpretability; NSD CLIP shows modest absolute performance on only 8 subjects
No analysis of learned representations (visualization, probing, or interpretation studies) to explain what structure the model captures beyond reconstruction accuracy
Incomplete experimental validation: missing comparisons to simpler baselines, limited robustness checks, no failure case analysis, and generalization to non-HCP preprocessing pipelines unclear

strengths: Novel flat map representation that creatively adapts cortical surface projections for Vision Transformers in fMRI, enabling practical scaling to 3D brain volumes
Comprehensive BrainMarks benchmark suite covering 7 datasets and diverse downstream tasks (trait prediction, state prediction, cognitive decoding, denoising), providing valuable community resource

Rigorous experimental methodology with proper train/test splits, multiple random seeds, extensive ablation studies (masking strategies, temporal patch size, normalization), and careful hyperparameter tuning
Thorough scaling analysis examining how fMRI foundation models scale with pretraining data size and model capacity, providing practical insights about representation effectiveness
Strong reproducibility: uses publicly available HCP data, provides detailed hyperparameters in appendices, documents computational requirements (~7K H100 hours), and adopts open-source approach
Systematic comparison across three representation types (parcel, flat map, volume), providing empirical insights into representation-task interactions across multiple datasets
weaknesses: Limited novelty: primarily adapts existing techniques (ViT, MAE) using well-established cortical surface projection approaches; no novel architectural innovations or fundamental methodological advances

Inconsistent empirical improvements: Table 2 shows flat maps provide modest benefits (often within error margins of volume models), contradicting claims of flat maps avoiding volume information loss; no model consistently outperforms baselines across datasets (Table 8)

Critical null results inadequately explained: models universally fail at state prediction (HCP-A age, sex, Task21 in Table 2), suggesting they may not capture important fMRI dynamics; this contradicts foundation model effectiveness claims but receives limited analysis

Mysterious failure of data augmentation (Table 4b): standard augmentation strategies (temporal rescaling, jitter) show almost no improvement, suggesting either pretraining saturation or augmentation unsuitability for fMRI—neither possibility is investigated

Limited applicability: flat map representation excludes subcortical structures by design; all experiments on healthy young adults (HCP-YA ages 22-35); clinical significance and generalization to patient populations never demonstrated

Incomplete justification for key design choices: why tube masking outperforms uniform masking by ~2x (Table 4a) is unexplained; the 'goldilocks zone' hypothesis is stated but not rigorously tested or validated

Contradictory findings on input normalization (Table 6): coordinate normalization during evaluation significantly hurts performance, yet methods describe using coordinate normalization during pretraining—inconsistency requires clarification

Insufficient analysis of representation-specific failure modes: different representations rank differently across tasks (Table 2), but no investigation into what different representations capture or why they fail on specific tasks
Sparse statistical significance testing and limited engagement with whether performance differences are meaningful or within noise margins across datasets

Missing computational efficiency guidance: while parcel MAE trains 2.5x faster (Table 3), paper doesn't provide clear recommendations for when practitioners should use which representation given accuracy-compute tradeoffs

strengths: Comprehensive benchmark suite (BRAINMARKS) spanning 8 datasets and multiple tasks is useful for the community
Thorough and honest reporting of null results and limitations rather than selective reporting
Extensive ablation studies examining mask sampling, normalization, architecture choices, and temporal dynamics
Excellent reproducibility: open-source code, detailed methods, extensive appendices, and transparent preprocessing pipelines
Systematic evaluation across trait prediction and state prediction tasks with proper statistical methodology (confidence intervals, random splits)
Well-motivated flat map representation achieves dimensionality reduction (~4-5x in sequence length) with technical soundness
weaknesses: Core claim fundamentally unsupported: authors explicitly state 'no single model achieves clear state-of-the-art performance' and models 'struggle to outperform a simple functional connectivity baseline,' contradicting the foundation model thesis

Weak and inconsistent scaling behavior (Figure 7c): downstream probe accuracy does NOT improve predictably with dataset size; NSD (largest) underperforms by ~10% compared to smaller datasets, contradicting expected foundation model properties
Poor generalization across datasets undermines transfer learning claims: UKBB pretraining underperforms HCP-YA pretraining on HCP-YA test set (Table 11)
Multiple prior models outperform CorTexMAE on several benchmarks: Brain-JEPA, BrainHarmony-F achieve better performance on multiple tasks (Figure 8, Table 14)
Limited technical novelty: primarily applies existing MAE-ViT framework to flat maps; cortical flat map representation borrowed from prior neuroscience work; no significant methodological innovations
Overstated foundation model framing inappropriate given results: genuine foundation models require strong transfer properties and consistent scaling, both absent here
Modest representation advantages: flat map vs. volume performance gap is small (Table 2: 87.4 vs 86.2 on HCP-A Age); insufficient justification for the 2D vs 3D tradeoff
Insufficient investigation of failure cases: no clear explanation for why NSD pretraining hurts generalization or why scaling laws are weak; these are critical gaps for claimed foundation models
Many results lack statistical clarity: differences often within confidence intervals (Figure 7, Table 2); claims sometimes overstate marginal improvements
Dataset preprocessing inconsistencies: different pipelines across datasets confound comparisons; different age distributions and experimental conditions inadequately controlled

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 8 datasets with multiple downstream tasks and systematic scaling analysis demonstrating rigor and thoroughness
Novel and well-motivated flat map representation elegantly bridges spatial detail and computational efficiency, showing empirical advantages over volume and parcellation approaches
Strong reproducibility and transparency: open-source code, detailed implementation details, BRAINMARKS benchmark creation, and honest discussion of limitations and failures
Practical significance as first systematic study of fMRI foundation models with proper scaling laws and benchmarking, creating valuable resources for the neuroscience-ML community
Clear presentation with informative visualizations, comprehensive tables, and logical progression from method through experiments to analysis
Honest reporting of inconsistent results across datasets and when foundation models underperform simpler baselines, strengthening credibility
Computational efficiency gains demonstrated (2.5× speedup vs volume models) with detailed cost analysis provided
weaknesses: Limited core technical novelty: straightforward application of standard masked autoencoders and Vision Transformers with primary innovation being the representation choice, which while sensible is somewhat incremental

Inconsistent and modest empirical improvements with model ranking varying across datasets and improvements often within confidence intervals; on some datasets (COCO24) foundation models barely exceed simple connectome baseline

Poor out-of-distribution generalization with significant performance drops on NSD/COCO24 despite HCP-YA pretraining, and model improvements varying by pretraining dataset; applicability to real-world clinical settings unclear

Critical findings inadequately explained: coordinate normalization improves training but hurts test performance (Table 15), data augmentation provides no benefit (Table 9), and input normalization choice dramatically affects results—suggesting hyperparameter sensitivity rather than fundamental insights

Data augmentation failure (Table 9) unexplored; the lack of improvement from TR scaling, aspect jittering, and intensity augmentation raises questions about whether models learn robust vs. dataset-specific features
Limited mechanistic understanding of why flat maps work: empirical advantage over volume/parcellation shown but the geometric or representational properties exploited by MAE not analyzed
Benchmark scope limitations: small sample sizes (minimum 16 subjects), limited acquisition diversity, no cross-site generalization analysis, and state prediction tasks underrepresented
Scaling behavior shows diminishing returns (power-law in Fig 7) and saturation around 50K parameters; unclear if massive pretraining investment justifies computational cost (~7K H100 hours)
Ethical considerations underexplored: implications of large-scale fMRI models for cognitive/emotional state inference and clinical deployment risks deserve deeper treatment
Dense presentation with important findings (e.g., pretraining dataset selection matters more than size) buried; main narrative could clearer state when and why foundation models help
